title: Cebu protest dispersal prompts calls for probe into alleged police brutality
summary: The November 16 protest dispersal in Cebu City raises questions about the PNP's adherence to its maximum tolerance policy and the Public Assembly Act

items: Civil society and academic groups in Cebu are calling for an impartial investigation into alleged human rights abuses and police brutality during a protest dispersal on November 16.
The Philippine National Police reported injuries among both protesters and police, while activists claim excessive force was used, including batons and shields against peaceful demonstrators.

Human rights lawyer Kristian Jacob Casas-Abad Lora argues that the police's intervention was unnecessary and that the burning of an effigy during the protest was a protected form of expression, not a public disturbance.

CEBU, Philippines – Several civil society and academic groups have called for an impartial investigation into alleged human rights abuses and police brutality during the dispersal of a protest in Cebu City on Monday, November 16.

The dispersal occurred on Monday afternoon when more than a hundred protesters expressed their dissent over the Pax Silica initiative and United States President Donald Trump’s visit in time for the 49th ASEAN summit.

“The University of the Philippines Cebu College of Communication, Art and Design (CCAD) also strongly condemns the violent dispersal of protesters in Colon, Cebu City, and the use of excessive force against individuals exercising their constitutional rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” the college’s statement read.

In a statement on November 17, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said that activists burned an effigy along a public road near Metro Gaisano Colon, claiming that there was a prior agreement not to proceed with the activity.

“The incident raised safety concerns due to electrical wires directly above the area. Some protesters also allegedly attempted to take a fire extinguisher from responding police personnel, resulting in a brief commotion,” the statement read.

Anthony Malibago of Karapatan Central Visayas told Rappler on Wednesday, November 18, that police grabbed a protester who tried to stop law enforcers from extinguishing a burning effigy, prompting other rallyists to form a barricade around the individual.

Progressive coalition BAYAN Central Visayas said police and protesters had reached no agreement on the burning of the effigy, adding that organizers had only committed to proper marshaling and compliance with traffic arrangements.

“We denounce the use of batons and shields and the attempted arrest of progressive organization members while the protest was still ongoing,” progressive coalition BAYAN Central Visayas said in their statement.

blocks.caption: EXTINGUISH. Police use a fire extinguisher on an effigy resulting in dense smoke covering parts of Colon Street. Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

blocks.text: According to the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) Cebu, the dispersal resulted in multiple injuries to protesters, including peasant advocates who were at the center of the confrontation.
Karapatan Central Visayas estimated that more than 20 rallyists were injured in the altercation while the PNP reported that two police personnel sustained injuries to their arms and hands.
The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) Cebu also reported injuries among members of the press during the protest.

“One journalist was wounded after being struck by a police shield. Another inhaled thick powder from a fire extinguisher discharged by police and feared for his health. Neither were severely injured, but we do not tolerate this violence,” the NUJP Cebu stated.

blocks.caption: BARRICADE. A group of activists hold on to one another as a police officer attempts to grab a slogan during an altercation in front of Metro Colon. Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

blocks.text: For human rights lawyer Kristian Jacob Casas-Abad Lora, the altercation and resulting injuries would not have occurred had police exercised maximum tolerance as required under Batas Pambansa 880 or the Public Assembly Act of 1985, or at least allowed the public assembly to finish as it was nearing the end of its program.
Lora said there was no clear and present danger for police to intervene as the fire was done in an open space and was containable.

“It is inaccurate for PNP Cebu City to say that burning of effigies is absolutely prohibited or illegal even under the antiquated Marcosian Batas Pambansa Blg. 880. Not all kinds of burning of any object during a public assembly are prohibited and penalized under the law,” Lora said.

The lawyer explained that the law only prohibits the malicious burning or burning with the intent of causing public disturbance or causing injury or damage to property. The burning of the effigy, he added, was a symbolic expression of sentiment — a part of protected speech — that was not intended to cause public disturbance, injury, or damage.
“It is clear that, even if the rally was with a permit, it was still the PNP’s intention to put out the fire and provoke the protesters so that there would be reason to arrest them,” Lora said.

“In fact, as video footage would show, even if the protesters had already dispersed themselves, police officers tried, again, to arrest, suddenly and forcibly, the participants who were already about to go home,” he added.
Rappler’s footage from the protest showed a police officer grabbing a female protester and another PNP personnel preparing to use his handgun.

blocks.text: Under BP 880, the carrying of firearms by members of the law enforcement unit within 100 meters from the area of activity of the public assembly constitutes a violation.
Police have denied carrying firearms or dragging protesters during the altercation.
As of Tuesday, police are investigating the incident and looking into filing charges against those who allegedly pushed police personnel during the protest.

“An investigation is underway to establish the full circumstances of the incident and identify those responsible for the alleged assault on police personnel and other possible violations of law,” the statement read.

In response, BAYAN Central Visayas denounced the reported “threat of charges” under Batas Pambansa 880, describing it as an “attempt to weaponize the law and suppress legitimate dissent against anti-people policies.”
The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) is set to look into possible human rights violations committed during protests staged by various groups nationwide since November 15. – Rappler.com
